title: MD5 Hash Generator: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. MD5 hash of any text — 32 hex characters, computed in your browser. Enter your text to hash and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Generate the MD5 hash of any text — a 32-character hex digest, computed entirely in your browser with a pure-JavaScript implementation of RFC 1321. The same input always gives the same hash, and even one changed character gives a completely different one, which is why MD5 is still used for checksums: comparing the hash of a downloaded file with the published one tells you whether the file arrived intact. MD5 is broken as a security hash, though — never use it for passwords or anything that must resist attack; use the SHA-256 generator for that.

## How to use the MD5 Hash Generator

Start by typing or pasting your text to hash. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Paste or type the text to hash.
2. Read the 32-character hex digest below.
3. Compare it with a published checksum to check a file or a value.

## Formula

MD5 (RFC 1321) pads the UTF-8 input to a multiple of 512 bits, then runs four rounds of 16 operations over the message blocks, producing a 128-bit digest shown as 32 hex characters.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The MD5 of “abc” is 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72, and the MD5 of the empty string is d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e. Change one letter and the hash changes completely. Try the same figures in the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Text to hash: abc), the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) returns MD5 hash: 900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72, Input length: 3 characters, 3 bytes (UTF-8), Algorithm: MD5 (RFC 1321), 128-bit. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [URL Encoder](/url-encoder) is worth a look before you finish.

## What MD5 is good for

Checksums and non-security identifiers. If you download a file and the publisher lists its MD5, hashing your copy and comparing the two values tells you whether the download is intact — an accidental corruption changes the hash completely. MD5 is also fast, which is why it still appears in databases and caches as a fingerprint for data that does not need to be tamper-proof.

## Why MD5 must not be used for security

MD5 has been cryptographically broken since 2004: researchers can create two different files with the same MD5 (a collision) in seconds, and precomputed tables make reversing common passwords trivial. Never store passwords as MD5, never use it to sign anything, and never trust it to prove a file came from someone — use SHA-256 or better for anything security-sensitive.

## How the hash is computed here

Web Crypto, the browser's built-in cryptography, deliberately has no MD5 — so this tool uses a compact pure-JavaScript implementation of RFC 1321, bundled with the site and tested against the RFC's own test vectors. The text is encoded as UTF-8 first, so accented characters and emoji hash the same way they do in standard tools.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The same input always gives the same hash — that is the point of a hash function.
- One changed character changes the whole digest: that is how checksums catch corruption.
- For passwords or signatures, use SHA-256 instead — MD5 is broken for security.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the MD5 of 'abc'?

900150983cd24fb0d6963f7d28e17f72. It is one of the standard test vectors for the algorithm, and this tool reproduces it exactly. Try it with your own numbers in the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Is MD5 secure?

No — MD5 has been cryptographically broken since 2004 and collisions can be made in seconds. It is fine for checksums and fingerprints, but never for passwords, signatures or anything security-sensitive. Use SHA-256 for those. Try it with your own numbers in the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why is the hash 32 characters long?

MD5 produces a 128-bit digest, and 128 bits written in hex is 32 characters. SHA-256 produces 256 bits, so its digest is 64 characters. Try it with your own numbers in the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What formula does the MD5 Hash Generator use?

MD5 (RFC 1321) pads the UTF-8 input to a multiple of 512 bits, then runs four rounds of 16 operations over the message blocks, producing a 128-bit digest shown as 32 hex characters. You can see it in action in the [MD5 Hash Generator](/md5-hash-generator) — enter your own values and the result updates as you type.
